extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in history, maritime disasters, and public-safety narratives
extracted.subtask_description: A narrative news/history article analyzing the causes and human factors behind the Costa Concordia cruise-ship disaster, emphasizing decisions, procedural failures, and legal outcomes. It explains what went wrong and who was held accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple causal factors / sequence of events
rubrics_metrics.description: “At any time when you have an incident similar to Concordia, there is never…a single causal factor. It is generally a sequence of events, things that line up in a bad way that ultimately create that incident.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat major incidents as chains of failures rather than single causes; investigators should look for how several errors and conditions combined to produce the disaster (quotes a U.S. Coast Guard senior marine inspector).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sail-by maneuver / sailing too close to the coastline
rubrics_metrics.description: Sailing close to shore to give passengers a view or salute other sailors is known as a “sail-by.” Italy’s Ministry of Infrastructures and Transports found that the Concordia “was sailing too close to the coastline, in a poorly lit shore area…at an unsafe distance at night time and at high speed (15.5 kts).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviation from planned route near shore, especially at night and in poorly lit areas, is flagged as a dangerous practice; investigators critique such discretionary close approaches as an avoidable risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviation from planned route for non-operational reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: The Concordia deviated from its planned path to sail closer to the island of Giglio, allegedly to salute other mariners or give passengers a good view; prosecutors alleged the captain sailed close to impress a woman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider intent and justification for route deviations—non-operational motives (showmanship, personal reasons) are treated as negligent if they increase risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsafe speed while near shore
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ministry report noted the ship was moving “at high speed (15.5 kts)” near the coastline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speed limits or prudent speed reductions near hazards/coastlines are a critical safety criterion; excessive speed reduces reaction time and increases likelihood/severity of impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collision with underwater hazards due to proximity (struck Scole Rocks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the ship sailed too close, it struck a reef known as the Scole Rocks; the impact damaged the ship, allowing water to seep in and endangering everyone on board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical consequences of risky navigation (hitting known hazards) are central evidence of causation — investigators link navigational choices directly to hull breach and flooding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Helmsman/crew response errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Captain Schettino blamed Helmsman Jacob Rusli Bin for reacting incorrectly to his order; the helmsman was late in executing the captain’s orders and was one of four crew members convicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess individual crew actions and timeliness of response; evaluate whether crew performance (delayed or incorrect execution of orders) contributed materially to the outcome, while also considering whether the incident was unavoidable even with timely action (as testified by an admiral).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delayed or inadequate notification to rescue authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Schettino didn’t immediately alert the Italian Search and Rescue Authority; the impact occurred ~9:45 p.m., Search and Rescue contacted the ship a few minutes after 10:00 p.m., but Schettino didn’t tell them what had happened for about 20 more minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely, accurate communication with rescue authorities is a key safety criterion; delays in notification impede prompt rescue and are treated as a serious procedural failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Downplaying/misrepresenting the incident and crisis management failures
rubrics_metrics.description: A recorded call shows Schettino tried to downplay and cover up his actions by saying the blackout caused the accident; Costa Crociere’s crisis coordinator Roberto Ferrarini tried to downplay the situation and was later convicted for contributing to the disaster by delaying rescue operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honest, transparent crisis reporting and effective crisis management are expected; attempts to misrepresent causes or minimize severity are considered aggravating misconduct and can worsen outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evacuation failures and procedural breakdowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Evacuation began a little more than an hour after impact; some passengers testified they didn’t hear the alarm; the ship listed heavily making movement difficult and lowering lifeboats on one side; the crew dropped the anchor incorrectly, causing the ship to flop over more dramatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective alarm procedures, lifeboat deployment, crew training, and correct use of equipment (anchor, davits) are essential; failures in any of these areas produce chaotic evacuation and increased casualties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captain abandoning ship / failure of command leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Through the confusion, the captain somehow made it into a lifeboat before everyone else had made it off; a coast guard member angrily told him to “Get back on board, damn it!”; the captain was found guilty of abandoning ship and sentenced to 16 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Command responsibility requires prioritizing passenger and crew safety and overseeing evacuation; abandoning command or failing to lead during evacuation is a grave breach of duty and a primary factor in assigning blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal accountability and criminal convictions for operational and managerial failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Italian courts found the captain, four crew members and one company official (Costa Crociere) at fault; convictions included manslaughter, causing a shipwreck, abandoning ship, and lying to authorities — sentencing (e.g., Schettino 16 years) is noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-incident evaluations include legal outcomes as evidence of responsibility; criminal convictions demonstrate how operational and managerial failures can translate into legal culpability and penalties.
